newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Tax revamp may hike Australia beer, tobacco prices.
newsitem.headline: Tax revamp may hike Australia beer, tobacco prices.

text.p: Australian beer and cigarette producers were seeking urgent meetings with government officials on Friday amid confusion about proposed tax changes which threaten to push up prices.
Two of Australia's big three cigarette manufacturers, Philip Morris Cos Inc's Australian unit and W.D. & H.O. Wills, have suspended sales to wholesalers and retailers.
Meanwhile, the two biggest brewers, Lion Nathan Ltd and Foster's Brewing Group, have wasted little time in passing on a new 15 percent tax to retailers.
Companies and industry associations are planning meetings in all states to try to sort out the problem, but have warned price rises will be inevitable if a quick solution is not found.
Cigarette stocks held by many retailers are expected to run out by Monday if a solution is not found.

The confusion flows from a High Court finding that about A$5 billion (US$3.65 billion) in franchise fees levied by the states on alcohol, tobacco and petrol were unconstitutional because they were in reality excise duties which only the Federal government could levy.
The Australian government agreed on Wednesday to replace the fees with new flat-rate national taxes which consist of a new 15 percent tax on beer and a higher excise on tobacco.

In theory, the goverment would collect the taxes and pass them on to the states. Each of the six states -- which have differing tax levels -- would have to return any excess funds to wholesalers to ensure the status quo.
Industry groups, however, say no arrangements have been put in place to return the difference between the new tax and the old state-based fees.

The tobacco industry believes the change to a tax based on weight, rather than price, will also lead to the collection of about A$500 million of extra taxes. It is also concerned some states will use higher tobacco taxes as a revenue boost to allow lower prices for other products.

Of the big three tobacoo makers, only Rothmans Holdings Ltd has decided to return operations to normal after a one-day suspension of deliveries. Wills Holdings is a subsidiary of the London-based giant B.A.T. Industries.
Major brewers have passed on the 15 percent tax rise to retailers, although retailers are yet to pass on the price rise to consumers.
Fosters' brewing arm, Carlton and United Breweries (CUB), said it planned a series of meetings with state governments to clarify how any refund system would work.

"What we are looking for is how any excess surplus funds are coming back in and putting that in place very quickly to make sure retailers don't have to pass the price rise on to consumers," said a CUB spokesman.
In New South Wales, the industry is angered that the government has indicated it will not refund about A$150 million in state licence fees which have been pre-paid for the next five months.

"As of yesterday morning liquor stores in this state are paying an extra 15 percent sales tax on goods that are being delivered to them, which means they are being double taxed," said Mal Higgs of the New South Wales Liquor Stores Association.
Theo Karedis, proprietor of the 29-store Theos liquor chain said his group was holding off on passing on the price rise to consumers until the outcome of industry talks.
However, he said retailers were likely to have to put up prices next week if the tax muddle could not be resolved.
"I don't want the public to suffer, but the industry shouldn't suffer either," he said.
